setup: Single-index model on excess returns. Security A: beta 0.80, residual volatility 15%. Security B: beta 1.10, residual volatility 30%. The market's volatility is 10%. All residuals are uncorrelated with each other and with the market. (The alphas do not matter here.)
ask: Is the correlation between A and B low (below 0.25) or high (above 0.5)?

options.label: High, above 0.5
options.why: Treated the shared market factor as the whole story. With no residual risk the correlation would be 1.0, but residual variance is about 78% of A's total and 88% of B's, and it is not shared.

takeaway: Only the market-factor part of risk is shared in a single-index model, so large residual variances pull the correlation down.

setup: One-factor regression of a portfolio on the market, monthly data. Beta 0.63, market volatility 9.0%, residual volatility 5.0%. The 50 bp alpha does not enter this step.
ask: What share of the portfolio's total variance does the market explain (R-squared)?

options.label: About 75%
options.why: Took the square root of $R^2$: that is the correlation with the market, not the explained share of variance.

options.label: About 63%
options.why: Read beta as if it were the explained share; beta is a slope, not a share of variance.

options.label: About 44%
options.why: Reported the residual share, $1 - R^2$, instead of the explained share.

takeaway: Explained variance over total variance is $R^2$; the correlation is its square root (0.75 here).

setup: Trade/no-trade rule for a stock: do nothing while $-SC \le \alpha - m \le PC$, where $m = 2\lambda_A\psi\,\text{MCAR}$ is the risk charge. Purchase cost PC = 0.30%, sales cost SC = 0.40%. At the start $m = 0.20\%$, so the band for alpha is $-0.20\%$ to $+0.50\%$. The manager's active risk aversion $\lambda_A$ now doubles; everything else is unchanged.
ask: What happens to the no-trade band for alpha?

options.label: Wider
options.why: Counted the bigger risk charge as widening the band. The width is always $PC + SC = 0.70\%$; $m$ only slides the band.

options.label: Same width, moved down
options.why: Got the direction of the shift backwards: $m$ enters the bounds with a plus sign, so a bigger $m$ lifts both ends.

takeaway: Risk aversion and MCAR shift the no-trade band; only trading costs set its width.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Pension fund, INR million. Assets 500, expected growth 8%, volatility 15%. Liabilities 410, expected growth 9%, volatility 8%. Asset return and liability growth are jointly normal with correlation 0.7. One-year horizon.
ask: The volatility of the end-of-year surplus, in INR million, is closest to:

options.why: Treated assets and liabilities as uncorrelated ($\rho = 0$): $\sqrt{75^2 + 32.8^2} = 81.9$.
Added the covariance term instead of subtracting it: $\sqrt{75^2 + 32.8^2 + 2(0.7)(75)(32.8)} = 100.7$.
Added the two dollar volatilities in a straight line, $75 + 32.8$, ignoring correlation altogether.

takeaway: Surplus is assets minus liabilities, so the covariance term is subtracted: positive correlation shrinks surplus risk.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A fund's VaR decomposition, % of assets, same confidence level and horizon: policy-mix VaR 19.6%, active-management VaR 1.6%, total asset VaR 19.3%. Total VaR combines the two components as $\text{VaR}_T^2 = \text{VaR}_P^2 + \text{VaR}_A^2 + 2\rho\,\text{VaR}_P\text{VaR}_A$.
ask: The implied correlation between the policy-mix and active components is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: If the two were uncorrelated the total would be $\sqrt{19.6^2 + 1.6^2} = 19.67\%$, above the stated 19.3%.

options.label: Positive
options.why: A positive correlation pushes the total even higher than 19.67%, and the stated total is below the policy-mix VaR alone.

takeaway: If total VaR is below even the larger component alone, the active bet must be diversifying: correlation is negative.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Pension fund with USD 600m of assets and USD 600m of liabilities, so the current surplus is zero. Assets: expected return 8%, volatility 18%. Liabilities: expected growth 6%, volatility 14%. Correlation 0.60, both normal. Use $z = 1.645$.
ask: The 95% absolute surplus at risk (worst shortfall against the current surplus of zero, after allowing for expected surplus growth) is closest to:

options.label: USD 12m
options.why: Stopped at the expected growth of the surplus ($48 - 36 = +12$), which is a gain, and never reached the risk term.

options.label: USD 40m
options.why: Combined the volatilities as a difference, $1.645 \times (108 - 84) = 39.5$, as if assets and liabilities were perfectly correlated.

options.label: USD 12,900m
options.why: Multiplied $z$ by the surplus variance (7,834) and forgot the square root.

takeaway: Absolute SaR is the relative SaR minus the expected surplus growth: positive drift eats into the shortfall.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Pension fund with a 50/50 equity and fixed income policy mix, held exactly (no deviation). Benchmark returns: equity 7.0%, fixed income 5.0%. The fund's managers returned 4.0% in equity and 10.0% in fixed income.
ask: The return attributable to active management is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Reasoned that holding the policy weights means no active effect. Weights match, but manager selection in each sleeve still adds or subtracts.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Looked only at the equity sleeve, $0.5 \times (4 - 7) = -1.5\%$, and stopped before adding the fixed income sleeve.

takeaway: Active return is the sum of each sleeve's weight times its manager-minus-benchmark gap; a big win in one sleeve can outweigh a loss in the other.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A pension plan has assets of USD 150m, all in equities, and liabilities of USD 120m with duration 14. Over the year the equity assets fall 30% and yields fall by 2 percentage points.
ask: The change in the value of the liabilities is closest to:

options.label: -USD 33.6m
options.why: Sign error: liabilities behave like a bond, so a fall in yields raises their value.

options.label: +USD 3.4m
options.why: Entered the 2-point yield change as 0.2% (0.002) instead of 2% (0.02): scale error by a factor of 10.

takeaway: Liabilities are bond-like: yields down means liability value up, which hurts the surplus twice when assets also fall.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A USD 10m fund is benchmarked to an index. Fund volatility is 10.0%, benchmark volatility 5.0%, and the fund's tracking error (volatility of fund minus benchmark) is 8.0%. All normal; use $z = 1.645$ at 95%.
ask: Compared with the fund's own absolute 95% VaR, its 95% tracking-error VaR is:

options.label: The same
options.why: Used the fund's 10% volatility for the relative VaR as well; relative VaR runs off the tracking error.

options.label: Larger
options.why: Added the fund and benchmark volatilities (10% + 5%) instead of using the tracking error: $1.645 \times 15\% \times 10 = 2.47$ (USD m).

takeaway: Relative VaR uses the volatility of the excess return (tracking error), not the fund's or the benchmark's own volatility.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A fund splits USD 400m between two active managers with independent excess returns and an index fund (zero tracking error). It maximises its portfolio information ratio subject to a total tracking error of 4%. Manager 1: TEV 8%, IR 0.48. Manager 2: TEV 6%, IR 0.36.
ask: The maximum portfolio information ratio is closest to:

options.why: Added the two information ratios; independent alphas combine in quadrature, not linearly.
Averaged the two information ratios, $(0.48 + 0.36)/2$.
Took the better manager's IR alone; combining two independent managers must improve on that.

takeaway: With independent managers the portfolio IR is the root of the sum of squared IRs, above the best single manager's IR.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Pension fund allocating USD 300m across two independent active managers and an index fund, maximising portfolio IR (0.72) at a total TEV of 4%. Manager 1: TEV 6%, IR 0.60. Manager 2: TEV 8%, IR 0.40. Optimal weight: $w_i = (IR_i/IR_P)(TEV_P/TEV_i)$.
ask: Manager 2's optimal allocation, compared with Manager 1's, is:

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed an equal split between the two active managers; the formula tilts toward higher IR and lower TEV.

options.label: Larger
options.why: Saw the higher TEV and assumed more room for risk. TEV sits in the denominator, so it cuts the weight, and Manager 2's IR is lower too.

takeaway: Optimal weight rises with IR and falls with TEV: a lower IR and a higher TEV both shrink the allocation.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Two equity managers each run USD 325m with volatility 15.8%; their returns have correlation 0.81. Using $z = 2.33$, each manager's VaR is $2.33 \times 0.158 \times 325 = 119.65$ (USD m). The fund's VaR for the USD 650m is $\text{VaR}_1\sqrt{2 + 2\rho}$.
ask: The factor $\sqrt{2 + 2\rho}$ that multiplies one manager's VaR is closest to:

options.why: Assumed perfect correlation ($\rho = 1$), which just adds the two VaRs in a straight line.
Assumed zero correlation, $\sqrt{2}$.
Computed $2 + 2\rho$ and forgot the square root.

takeaway: Between the no-diversification factor 2.00 and the zero-correlation factor 1.41, a correlation of 0.81 sits close to the top.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A pension fund holds USD 28.0bn in equities with volatility 14.0%. Its 95% one-year VaR (use $z = 1.645$) is $1.645 \times 0.14 \times 28.0 = 6.45$ (USD bn). The VaR is divided between two managers with identical budgets, whose returns have correlation 0.30.
ask: Each manager's VaR budget, compared with half the fund VaR (USD 3.22bn), is:

options.label: Exactly half
options.why: Assumed budgets simply add up, which is true only at correlation 1. At 0.30 the combination is smaller than the sum.

options.label: Less than half
options.why: Thought diversification shrinks each manager's budget; it does the opposite, since the two budgets must sum to more than the fund VaR.

takeaway: With correlation below 1 the equal budgets sum to more than the fund VaR, so each exceeds half of it.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: Delta-normal VaR at 99% ($z = 2.326$) for a EUR 100m fund with a total volatility target of 5%. Four asset classes (weights 40%, 12%, 22%, 26%; volatilities 9.25%, 11.91%, 5.76%, 11.94%) with pairwise correlations between -0.07 and +0.02. A class's risk budget is its share of the diversified fund VaR. The four stand-alone VaRs add up to EUR 22.10m.
ask: The four risk budgets together add up to:

options.label: Exactly 22.10m
options.why: Added the stand-alone VaRs. That ignores diversification, so it overstates the fund VaR the budgets must add up to.

options.label: More than 22.10m
options.why: Budgets cannot exceed the stand-alone total; with near-zero correlations they are smaller still.

takeaway: Risk budgets decompose the diversified fund VaR, so they sum to it, well below the sum of stand-alone VaRs.

reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
setup: A fund uses three managers with uncorrelated active returns: A (50% of the fund, tracking error 4.0%), B (30%, 6.0%), C (20%, 3.0%). Fund tracking-error variance is the sum of each manager's (weight x TE)$^2$.
ask: Which manager contributes the most to the fund's tracking-error variance?

options.label: Manager B
options.why: Ranked by raw tracking error (6.0%, the highest) and ignored weights: B contributes $(0.3 \times 6)^2 = 3.24$ against A's 4.00.

options.label: Manager C
options.why: Reversed the ranking: C's $(0.2 \times 3)^2 = 0.36$ is the smallest contribution.

takeaway: Contribution to variance is (weight x TE) squared: a large weight can outweigh a higher stand-alone TE.

setup: A fund grew from 100 to 175 over 30 months, so its geometric monthly return is 1.88%. Monthly returns are normal with a monthly standard deviation of 10.0%. The arithmetic mean is estimated as $R_A \approx R_G + \tfrac12\sigma^2$.
ask: The volatility term $\tfrac12\sigma^2$, per month, is closest to:

options.why: Squared the 1.88% geometric return instead of the 10% volatility: $0.5 \times (1.88\%)^2 = 0.018\%$.
Halved the volatility instead of the variance: $0.5 \times 10\% = 5\%$.
Used $\sigma = 10$ in percent units, squared it and halved it without rescaling: $0.5 \times 10^2 = 50$.

takeaway: The arithmetic mean exceeds the geometric mean by about half the variance; with 10% monthly volatility that is 0.5% a month.

setup: Buy one share at USD 40. It pays a USD 4 dividend each year. At the end of year 1, after receiving that dividend, buy a second share at USD 42. At the end of year 2, collect the dividend on both shares and sell both at USD 43. We are building the cash-flow chain for the dollar-weighted return.
ask: The net cash flow to the investor at the end of year 1 is:

options.label: -USD 42
options.why: Counted only the purchase and left out the USD 4 dividend received at the same date.

options.label: -USD 46
options.why: Subtracted the dividend instead of adding it: $-42 - 4$.

options.label: +USD 4
options.why: Counted only the dividend and forgot the purchase of the second share.

takeaway: Net all flows that fall on the same date before solving for the IRR: dividend in, purchase out.

setup: An investor bought 500 shares at USD 60 on 1 Jan 2016 and 500 more at USD 75 on 1 Jan 2017. A USD 5 per-share dividend was paid at the end of each year. All 1,000 shares were sold at USD 90 on 31 Dec 2017. The time-weighted return chains each year's holding-period return (HPR), measured per share.
ask: The year-2 HPR (from USD 75 at the start of 2017) is closest to:

options.why: Price gain only, $(90 - 75)/75$; the USD 5 dividend is left out.
Divided the USD 20 gain by the ending price of USD 90 instead of the starting price of USD 75.
That is the year-1 HPR, $(75 - 60 + 5)/60$.

takeaway: An HPR is gain plus income over the starting value of that period, per share, so share count does not matter.
